extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing patent eligibility under 35 U.S.C. §101, with emphasis on software-related inventions and how to apply the Office's Alice/Mayo (Step 2A/2B) framework and MPEP §2106 guidance. Includes examples of precedential Federal Circuit decisions illustrating eligible and ineligible outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use current subject matter eligibility guidance (MPEP §2106)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should assess patent eligibility in view of the current subject matter eligibility guidance, which has been integrated into the MPEP (particularly MPEP §2106).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §2106.04(a)(1) for abstract ideas and MPEP §2106.06(b) for improvements to computer functionality. The Office's guidance maps to the Alice/Mayo framework (Step 2A and Step 2B). Follow the integrated MPEP guidance when analyzing claims for §101 issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Software inventions can be eligible when they make non-abstract improvements to computer technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Software-based innovations can make "non-abstract improvements to computer technology" and be deemed patent-eligible subject matter at the first step of the Alice/Mayo analysis (Step 2A in the Office's guidance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims directed to improvements in computer functionality may be found not to be directed to an abstract idea. Use decisions such as Enfish, McRO, Finjan, and Core Wireless as examples where software claims were held eligible because they improved computer technology rather than claiming an abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims directed to an abstract idea require an inventive concept to be eligible (MPEP §2106.05)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim is directed to an abstract idea, it must include an 'inventive concept' to transform the abstract idea into patent-eligible subject matter (see MPEP §2106.05).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precedential Federal Circuit cases have found claims ineligible as directed to abstract ideas without inventive concept (e.g., Inventor Holdings; Two-Way Media; Smart Systems Innovations; Secured Mail Solutions). When a claim's substance maps to those abstract-idea holdings, evaluate whether additional claim elements contribute an inventive concept beyond the abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate whether claims recite specific steps that accomplish a result improving computer functionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that recite specific steps producing a technical result that realizes an improvement in computer functionality are more likely to be patent eligible (e.g., Finjan).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Finjan, the method 'scans an application program, generates a security profile identifying any potentially suspicious code in the program, and links the security profile to the application program' — the court found these specific steps effected an improvement (protecting against unknown viruses and obfuscated code) compared to traditional virus scanning. Look for claim language that details how the improvement is achieved and what technical problem is solved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine whether claimed GUI or interface features constitute an improvement to electronic device functionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Graphical user interface claims may be eligible when directed to an improved user interface for electronic devices rather than an abstract idea (e.g., Core Wireless).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Core Wireless' claims (displaying an application summary of each application on the main menu while applications are in an unlaunched state) were held eligible because the claims contained precise language delimiting the type of data to be displayed and how to display it, resulting in increased efficiency. Examine claim precision about data types, display behavior, and how the interface improves device operation or user efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare claimed improvements to precedent (Enfish, McRO, Thales, Visual Memory, Finjan)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use existing Federal Circuit decisions that found eligibility for improved systems as comparators when determining if a software claim is directed to an improvement in computer functionality rather than an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The memorandum explicitly compares eligible GUI and software-improvement claims to Enfish, Thales, Visual Memory, and Finjan. Use factual and claim-scope parallels to inform whether a claimed invention aligns with these precedents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize common abstract-idea fact patterns that have been held ineligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware of abstract-idea subject matter categories and fact patterns that the Federal Circuit has recently found ineligible, such as local processing of payments for remote purchases, monitoring/delivery/accumulation of information, collection/storage/recognition of financial-transaction data for mass transit, and using markings on mail to communicate information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The memorandum cites specific cases as examples: Inventor Holdings (local processing of payments), Two‑Way Media (sending/directing/monitoring/accumulating information), Smart Systems Innovations (collection/storage/recognition of transaction data), Secured Mail Solutions (marking affixed to mail object). If claim substance maps to these types of abstract-idea holdings without additional inventive concept, treat as likely ineligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the USPTO Chart of Subject Matter Eligibility Decisions and Eligibility Quick Reference Sheet
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference the Office's Chart of Subject Matter Eligibility Decisions and the Eligibility Quick Reference Sheet, which are updated monthly, to inform §101 analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These resources summarize precedential and informative decisions and should be consulted when applying MPEP §2106 guidance and when comparing claim facts to prior case law examples.
